cues.text: Welcome to Network Architecture and Protocols, session six.
Today we look at emerging networks, starting with network virtualisation.
Instead of treating every physical cable and switch as its own separate network, we build logical networks on top of shared infrastructure.
The underlay is the physical IP transport.
An overlay encapsulates traffic to create logical connectivity across that transport.
VLANs segment local layer two networks; VXLAN carries Ethernet frames inside UDP and IP.
Its twenty-four-bit virtual network identifier, or VNI, allows roughly sixteen million identifiers.
VXLAN tunnel endpoints encapsulate and decapsulate the frames.
GRE can also encapsulate network protocols across IP paths, but it is not inherently encrypted.
Remember that extra headers take space, so plan the MTU and verify underlay reachability.
EVPN can distribute overlay reachability and control information.
Virtual switches and routers connect workloads, but isolation depends on actual security policy, not merely on network labels.

Network Functions Virtualisation, or NFV, takes functions such as firewalls, routers, load balancers and mobile-core functions and implements them in software on commodity or virtualised infrastructure.
In the ETSI reference architecture, a VNF is a virtual network function.
NFVI is the infrastructure: compute, storage, network resources and the virtualisation layer.
MANO stands for management and orchestration.
The NFV orchestrator, NFVO, coordinates orchestration; the VNF manager, VNFM, handles function lifecycle; and the virtualised infrastructure manager, VIM, manages infrastructure resources.
Cloud-native network functions can use containers, and are called CNFs.
SDN programmes connectivity while NFV virtualises functions.
They complement each other.
Consider performance, acceleration, resource isolation, orchestration, interoperability, lifecycle management and security.

Cloud networking gives us virtual networks, such as a VPC or VNet, with subnets, route tables, security groups, access control lists, gateways, VPN or private links, DNS, load balancers and peering or transit.
Infrastructure as a service supplies infrastructure resources.
Networking as a service supplies network capabilities; managed cloud networking abstracts some operations.
Public, private and hybrid clouds differ in ownership and deployment; multi-cloud uses multiple providers.
SD-WAN applies policies and software-managed path selection across wide-area links.
It is not automatically private or encrypted.

Cloud benefits include elasticity, provisioning, geographic reach and managed services, but dependence on providers, egress costs, misconfiguration, latency, data sovereignty and shared responsibility are real trade-offs.
Design redundant routes, avoid overlapping addresses, use private endpoints where appropriate, enforce least privilege and verify failover.
